assertions.text: Fulfillment method splitting is represented as its own table — items with different fulfillment types (store pickup vs home delivery) cannot share a shipment.
assertions.evidence: A dedicated 'Fulfillment Method Split' table is provided with scenarios showing that items with different fulfillment types result in separate shipments. For example, 'One delivery, one pickup' scenario shows 'Shirt, Mug' with 'Home delivery, Store pickup' resulting in '2' shipments.

assertions.text: Delivery address splitting is represented as its own table — items going to different addresses must be in separate shipments.
assertions.evidence: A dedicated 'Multi-Address Split' table is provided showing that items to different addresses create separate shipments. For example, 'Two items to different addresses' shows 'Shirt, Book' to 'Friend's house, Home' resulting in '2' shipments grouped as '[Shirt → Friend's], [Book → Home]'.

assertions.text: Availability splitting is represented as its own table — in-stock items ship immediately, backordered/pre-ordered items ship when available.
assertions.evidence: A dedicated 'Availability-Based Timing Split' table is provided. The table demonstrates that in-stock items have dispatch timing 'Immediately' while pre-order/backorder items have delayed timing (e.g., 'Pre-order 2026-05-01'). The scenario 'In-stock and pre-order' shows these split into '2' shipments with different dispatch times.

assertions.text: Warehouse allocation (minimising shipments) is represented as its own table — choosing which warehouses to ship from to minimise total shipment count.
assertions.evidence: A dedicated 'Warehouse Inventory Allocation' table is provided with a 'Min Shipments?' column. Scenarios explicitly demonstrate minimization logic: 'One warehouse overshoots — not needed' shows using 1 warehouse instead of 2, and 'Two-warehouse combo preferred over three' shows selecting 2 warehouses over more options.

assertions.text: Companion product grouping is represented as its own table — paired items (e.g. camera body and lens) should ship together from the same location when possible.
assertions.evidence: A dedicated 'Companion Product Constraint' table is provided with scenarios showing camera body and lens as companion pairs. Scenarios show when companions can ship together ('Both companions stocked at one warehouse', 'Companion warehouse preferred when a closer split exists') and when unavoidable splits occur.

assertions.text: Fulfillment table covers at least: all items for home delivery, all items for store pickup, and a mix of delivery and pickup items.
assertions.evidence: The Fulfillment Method Split table includes: 'All home delivery' scenario with 'Shirt, Trousers' both as 'Home delivery, Home delivery'; 'All store pickup' scenario with 'Shirt, Mug' both as 'Store pickup, Store pickup'; and 'One delivery, one pickup' scenario with mixed methods.

assertions.text: Delivery address table covers at least: all items to the same address, and items to different addresses.
assertions.evidence: The Multi-Address Split table includes 'All items to same address' scenario where 'Shirt, Book' go to 'Home, Home', and 'Two items to different addresses' scenario where 'Shirt, Book' go to 'Friend's house, Home'.

assertions.text: Availability table covers at least: all items in stock, a mix of in-stock and pre-order/backorder, and two backordered/pre-ordered items with different dates. Pre-order and backorder are recognised as equivalent for splitting semantics — either by comment, note, or by including both with the same rules.
assertions.evidence: The Availability-Based Timing Split table includes: 'All items in stock' with 'In stock, In stock'; 'Two pre-orders, different dates' with 'Pre-order 2026-04-15, Pre-order 2026-05-01' resulting in '2' shipments; and both 'In-stock and pre-order' and 'In-stock and backorder' scenarios showing both states treated equivalently with split shipments and different dispatch timings.

assertions.text: Warehouse allocation table covers at least: single warehouse has full quantity, multi-warehouse split needed, fewer-warehouse split preferred over more warehouses, and cannot fulfill (insufficient total stock).
assertions.evidence: The Warehouse Inventory Allocation table includes: 'One warehouse covers full order' with 'Chicago: 6' providing full quantity as '1' shipment; 'Two warehouses together cover order' requiring '2' shipments; 'Two-warehouse combo preferred over three' showing minimization; and 'Total stock below order quantity' with 'Chicago: 3, LA: 2' (total 5 < 6 ordered) marked as 'no' fulfillable.

assertions.text: Companion table covers at least: single warehouse has both companions, unavoidable split (no warehouse has both but both are available), and fulfillment not possible (one companion not available anywhere).
assertions.evidence: The Companion Product Constraint table includes scenarios for 'Both companions stocked at one warehouse' and 'No single warehouse stocks both companions' (unavoidable split), but lacks a scenario where one companion is not available anywhere (e.g., Camera body available but Lens unavailable everywhere, making fulfillment impossible).

assertions.text: Scenario names describe the business situation (e.g. 'Consolidate: two beats three', 'Everything at one warehouse') — not 'Test case 2'.
assertions.evidence: All scenario names across the five tables describe business situations: 'All home delivery', 'One delivery, one pickup', 'All items in stock', 'Two warehouses together cover order', 'Two-warehouse combo preferred over three', 'All items to same address', 'No single warehouse stocks both companions', etc. None use generic test case labels.

assertions.text: Trigger tables represent multi-item orders where each item has its own fulfillment type, address, and availability. The notation makes the item-to-property mapping unambiguous — not value sets like {delivery, pickup} which lose which item has which property.
assertions.evidence: Tables use comma-separated lists where item order matches property order, making mapping unambiguous. For example, Fulfillment table shows 'Shirt, Trousers' | 'Home delivery, Home delivery' and 'Shirt, Mug' | 'Home delivery, Store pickup', clearly pairing each item with its corresponding property.

assertions.text: Warehouse allocation table uses a scalar count column (e.g. 'Qty ordered') not item lists, when product identity doesn't matter for the logic.
assertions.evidence: The Warehouse Inventory Allocation table uses 'Qty Ordered' column with scalar values (6, 6, 4, 6, 6, 6) rather than item lists, since the scenarios deal with abstract quantity splitting logic across warehouses.

assertions.text: Column names use business/domain language (e.g. 'Shipments?' not 'Result?', 'Warehouse stock' not 'inventory_map'). The tables read as a specification a product person could review.
assertions.evidence: Column names throughout use business language: 'Fulfillment Methods', 'Shipments?', 'Grouped As?', 'Dispatch Timing?', 'Qty Ordered', 'Available Warehouses', 'Min Shipments?', 'Fulfillable?', 'Delivery Addresses', 'Warehouse Stock', 'Companions Same Shipment?'. All use domain-appropriate terms a product person would recognize.

assertions.text: Output/expected columns end with '?' (e.g. 'Shipments?', 'Groups?') to distinguish them from input columns.
assertions.evidence: All output/expected columns consistently end with '?': 'Shipments?', 'Grouped As?', 'Dispatch Timing?', 'Min Shipments?', 'Fulfillable?', 'Companions Same Shipment?' across all five tables, while input columns like 'Items', 'Fulfillment Methods', 'Availability', 'Warehouse Stock' do not.

assertions.text: Inventory assignments are physically valid: items are only assigned to locations that have them. Shipment counts match the assignments shown.
assertions.evidence: Warehouse scenarios show physically valid assignments: 'One warehouse overshoots' assigns Shirt qty 4 to Chicago which has 4, resulting in 1 shipment; 'Two-warehouse combo preferred over three' achieves qty 6 with 'Philly + Washington' (3+3=6) in 2 shipments; 'Only a three-warehouse combination' uses Chicago: 4, LA: 1, Houston: 1 (total 6) in 3 shipments; 'Total stock below order' correctly shows 'no' as unfulfillable.

assertions.text: Multiple open questions are surfaced across the tables — ambiguities, edge cases, or product decisions that the requirements don't fully specify.
assertions.evidence: An explicit 'Open Questions' section lists five questions: 'Companions forced to split' (warning, silent, or reject?), 'Companion + address conflict' (override rules?), 'Compound split reasons' (resolution order?), 'Multiple pickup locations' (separate shipments or blocked?), and 'Companion + inventory allocation' (priority trade-off?).
